content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper considers the problem of adapting an egocentric action recognition system to new environments. Specifically, the paper relies on ORViT for action recognition. ORViT is an action recognition method based on transformers which expects as input RGB observations (videos) and bounding box locations of objects in the input frames. When paired with a class agnostic hand-object recognition algorithm such as the one proposed in (Shan et al. 2020), ORViT can perform action recognition without any knowledge on the object taxonomy in the source or target environments. The paper hence shows that fine-tuning the hand-object recognition algorithm with a subset of labeled frames in the target environment allows to improve generalization. Experiments are performed in two settings: environment generalization within the Epic-Kitchens dataset, and environment generalization across the Epic-Kitchens and EGTEA Gaze+ datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
I found the overall investigation very interesting. Several works have shown the importance of dealing with objects when performing egocentric action anticipation, hence performing a domain adaptation approach based on the explicit adaptation of an object detection component to new objects appearing in the target environment is surely compelling. Moreover, object detectors can be used to tackle also other tasks, hence we can expect to re-use the adapted detector for additional downstream tasks (e.g., action anticipation, augmented reality, etc.). The reported experiments do make a point: adapting the object detector allows to improve the performance of the action recognition system in two challenging settings (within and across dataset scenario generalization). Experiments reported in Table 6 are convincing and nicely show the effect of combining the proposed adaptation technique with fine-tuning of the action recognition algorithms.

Nevertheless, I think the paper has some limitations which need to be addressed to make this a strong submission:
 - While the experiments do make a point as described above, there is no real comparison with other domain adaptation approaches in the paper. Indeed, previous works have considered an unsupervised domain adaptation scenario in which videos from the target domain do not have any labels. While these settings are more challenging than the proposed one in which a subset of labeled target images is available, it would be nevertheless useful to show how the proposed approach compares with respect to current art. Methods to consider would be the ones mentioned in section 4, e.g., (Jamal et al.; 2018), (Chen et al.; 2019), (Munro & Damen, 2020), (Pan et al., 2020). It could be also interesting to see how such methods combined with the proposed approach can affect performance. These experiments are important to understand the positioning of the paper with respect to the state of the art.
 - The paper mentions an "environment generalization" problem. However, the considered experiments actually consider more a "scenario generalization" in which not only the environment, but also the subjects and objects change. This is probably the main reason why adapting an object detector gives improvements in these settings. Imagine a scenario in which the same subject uses the same objects in a different environment. Would the proposed technique give similar performance boosts in this case as well? I am not sure if data fully reflecting these settings actually exists, but the EPIC-KITCHENS-100 dataset has a few subjects who recorded in different kitchens (not sure if the objects are the same or if they change). It may be worth to have a look at that data as well. While I find these settings very interesting, maybe referring to them simply as environment generalization could be misleading. Can the authors comment on this?
 - In the introduction, the paper states "Naturally, this will require some annotated images with the localized objects representative of the environment. But such supervision cost is much lower than that of a conventional approach described above.". It would be nice to see a quantitative comparison of the amount of time needed to provide temporal segment supervision vs hand-object interaction supervision. From section 2.2, it seems to me that for each frame labelers need to annotate objects, hands, and contact states, which may be time consuming as well.

Other notes and suggestions for extension:
 - The paper focuses on an egocentric scenario, even if this is not explicitly stated in the paper. How would this transfer to a classic third-person scenario? In that case, the hand-object detector could be replaced by a human-object interaction approach detecting the human (rather than the hand) and the interacted objects. It would be interesting to see such an investigation in the paper. An interesting scenario to consider could be the one of the breakfast dataset (https://serre-lab.clps.brown.edu/resource/breakfast-actions-dataset/).
 - On a similar note, I wonder if the hand-object detector could actually be fine-tuned (Section 2.3) if only object bounding boxes (hence not hands and contact states) were available. Indeed, object bounding boxes are much cheaper to collect and may already be available in some scenarios (e.g., EPIC-KITCHENS already has object bounding boxes). If it can be fine-tuned in such a way, it would be interesting to see how performance improvements are affected.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is overall well written and easy to follow. While the technical novelty is not vey high, I found the paper conceptually interesting. The authors release their code and the methods seems to be easily replicable to me.

Some minor comments:
 - Is "source environments" on the right part of Figure 1 correct? Or should it be "target environemnts"?
 - I wonder how is the procedure described in Section 2.3 similar to just performing classic fine-tuning of the hand-object detector using the procedures described in (Shan et al.; 2020). Can authors clarify that?
 - In section 3.4.1, "Table 3.4.1" should maybe be "Table 5"?
content.summary_of_the_review: I overall found the main idea behind the paper compelling. The reported experiments are well executed and do make a point. However, the lack of comparison with respect to state-of-the-art domain adaptation techniques makes the paper somewhat weak. What if the same results could be achieved in an unsupervised domain adaptation setting, i.e., without any labeled data in the target environments? Without this kind of experiments, it is hard to assess the positioning of the proposed work with respect to the state of the art, which makes this submission somewhat weak.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper describes a method based on ORViT that adapts only the class-specific object localization to transfer action recognition capability to a set of 4 net environments on standard kitchen activity recognition datasets.  The work is evaluated vs. fine-tuning with various amounts of annotated data within and between two kitchen datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses: The biggest strength is also the biggest weakness.  This paper is based on a fairly simplistic concept.  It does appear to improve performance with little cost, but the improvement is not overwhelming.  It would be good to understand the cost of annotation in hours and how much is saved versus performance.  It would be interesting to hear the authors impression of what is most surprising in the results.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The authors have promised to share the code and data for this paper, so it should be reproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall this paper is reasonable, but does not meet the high standards of contributions and improvements for ICLR paper acceptance. content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes an approach to adapt an action recognition model, which contains a category-agnostic object detector and action recognizer, to a new environment. The insight is that the action recognizer can be re-used and we only need to adapt the object detector. To do so, we simply need to fine-tune the model using object annotations collected in the new environment. The authors argue that the cost of collecting object annotations is lower than video-level action labels.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
The idea of adapting the object detector only is intriguing. This paper shows that the action recognizer can be reused. Also, simply fine-tuning the object detector can save a lot of computation.

Weaknesses:
1. An important baseline is missing: unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA). For example, adversarial loss is a commonly used approach for UDA. The idea is you train a domain classifier (if an image is from the source or target domain). When you train the object detector, the learned representations should not only work well for object detection, but also indistinguishable for the domain classifier. In this way, the learned object detector will also work well in a new environment and does not need to collect any object annotations. See details in [Yuhua Chen, Wen Li, Christos Sakaridis, Dengxin Dai, and Luc Van Gool. Domain adaptive faster
R-CNN for object detection in the wild. In CVPR, 2018].

2. The paper assumes the source domain and target domain have the same vocabulary for action recognition. But it may not always be the case in practice. For example, you may see novel objects in a new kitchen. As a result, you can not simply re-use the object detector. Fine-tuning the action recognizer is also needed.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper is clearly written and easy to follow. It is relatively novel and should not be hard to reproduce. The authors promise to release the code upon acceptance.
content.summary_of_the_review:
My main concerns are:
1. Lack of important baselines.
2. It does not work well for an environment that has different action vocabulary.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presented an approach to adapt pre-trained action recognition modes to a new environment. The assumption is that an object localization module, presented in the recognition model, can be leveraged for adaptation. Specifically, the paper proposed to only fine-tune the object localization module using sparsely sampled video frames and their annotated object bounding boxes from the new environment. The proposed method is evaluated on two egocentric action recognition datasets and demonstrates promising results. In particular, the results show that adapting using sparse object labels can achieve competitive results in comparison to fine-tuning the recognition model using data from the new environment.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strength**

The paper addresses a practical problem of adapting action recognition models to new environments and presents an interesting solution supported by comprehensive experiments. 

The key idea of adapting an action recognition model using sparse annotation of objects is interesting, novel and seems effective. 

The paper is well written and well executed. The text is easy to follow and the results are extensive. 

**Weakness**

I am not sure I understand why the proposed method works. Consider an action recognition model with an object centric representation (i.e., using an object localization module). To adapt this model to a new dataset, one can either better localize the object boxes (as proposed in this paper), or fine-tune the feature representations (as the common practice for transfer learning), or do both. It is not immediately clear why more accurate localization can offer better performance than fine-tuning the features, especially when the object appearance varies drastically (e.g., transfer from EPIC-Kitchens to EGTEA+). By looking at the object detection results in the Appendix (C.1 and C.2), it looks like the initial localization module is rather inaccurate, and fine-tuning is critical to improve the object localization performance. If that is the main reason, there seems to be other alternative solutions. 

For example, the only instantiation of the proposed method is based on ORViT, where object information (e.g., bounding boxes) is injected in early layers of the model. What if other object centric representations are adapted, e.g., injecting object boxes in middle layers (Arnab et al., 2021b) or mixing object centric representation and video features (Wang and Gupta, 2018)? These representations, by their design, might be more robust to inaccurate localization results. It will be great if the authors can demonstrate their findings on at least one of the other instantiations of the key idea. 

The proposed method seems to assume that the new environment will share the same action categories as the training dataset. The assumption itself is mostly fine, yet needs to be clearly discussed. For example, this assumption does bring a disadvantage to the proposed method. While the traditional fine-tuning can deal with new categories, the proposed method can not.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is well packaged with a key idea that is interesting and novel, despite that some of the alternative solutions are not well explored. Implementation details are described in the paper to ensure reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: The key idea of the paper is exciting. Yet I am not totally convinced by the current design and experimental results. At its current form, I am hesitant to recommend an accept. I am willing to reconsider my rating if the authors can address my concerns in the comments.
